item.title: The best take on the Hegseth Impeachment vote.
item.description:
Marisa Kabas is an independent journalist who publishes on https://www.thehandbasket.co/ and provides informed takes from a progressive POV. I think this is the best take on tonight's Hegseth vote, posted in the spirit of "bottom line up front."
To make sense of what happened: this is a lame duck session. Think of it like an office where half of the people just gave two-month's notice and are now dedicated solely to chillin' in the snack room. It is still the Republican-controlled Congress; the Blue Tsunami Congress isn't sworn in until January. So Dems knew that even if they all showed up to vote, the Republicans would just call their missing members to come downstairs and outvote them. You can argue they should have showed up anyway, and I agree, but that's not what this post is about. It's just about the logistics and ramifications of what happened. This was not "should we impeach?" It was "should the articles of impeachment be sent to the House Judiciary Committee for discussion?" Referring bills to committee is the process of taking a bill and refining it before it gets debated and voted on. This is a normal process for responsible legislating that also gets exploited to delay floor votes. This is why R's voted Yes and D's + Massie voted No. And the outcome was always going to be "send it to committee." Again, this is still the Republican-controlled Congress. The reason it was filed now, and not in January, is because Massie lost his seat, so he'll be out in January, so he filed them now. From the Dem's point of view, there wasn't any good reason to stop him, and even trying to stop him would have been A Bad Look. So this vote means the articles of impeachment will be sitting in the House Judiciary's docket in January EDIT: Actually, no it won't. As @InterTakerWeb and @UprootedGrunt, pointed out, bills in committee die when the Congress turns over. That was something I misunderstood! However, when the Blue Tsunami Congress is sworn in, articles of impeachment can be reintroduced. Many of the House reps have seen this process dozens of times, know it's bureaucratic stalling, and knew what the outcome would be. Which is probably why they weren't on the floor. But, as Kabas points out, this means they were treating this as normal, boring, bullshit business as usual. And, as Kabas points out, something is clearly different now. In the past, this process has flown under the radar. But now people are - probably for the first time! Admit it, you've never thought about this before - paying attention to who is and isn't voting. My personal additional take on this is: it's a good thing everyone's mad, even if maybe they don't need to be. Most normal people have never really had reason or motivation to learn the details of how Congress works, but things are different now.

item.title: Kash Patel Discovers the Fuck Around and Find Out Clause.
item.description:
There's a wonderful little feature of the American legal system that Kash Patel apparently overlooked. **When you sue someone, they get to defend themselves.** I know. Outrageous. Someone should investigate the bastard who came up with that.
Patel sued *The Atlantic* for defamation. Fair enough. That's his right. But then the magazine did something absolutely scandalous. It asked for evidence. Records. Calendars. Travel details. Information potentially relevant to the lawsuit. You know, the sort of material the FBI might ordinarily obtain when investigating somebody else. Suddenly, Patel discovered a passionate, almost religious devotion to personal privacy. The man running the FBI was concerned about people looking through his records. **THE FUCKING FBI.** An organization whose entire business model involves asking questions people would rather not answer. And when Patel objected, Judge Emmet Sullivan allowed *The Atlantic* to begin pursuing discovery. Not unlimited access. Not a ruling that every requested document must be surrendered. Just the ordinary legal process Patel himself set in motion. Which brings us to the bicycle. Kash climbs aboard, proudly announces his defamation lawsuit, jams a stick into the front wheel, and goes sailing over the handlebars. Then, from somewhere in the roadside shrubbery: **"WHO THE FUCK AUTHORIZED THIS INVESTIGATION?!"** You did, Kash. You magnificent, self-inflicted legal traffic accident. The courts aren't your personal complaint department, and discovery isn't an optional feature you can uninstall when the questions become inconvenient. **You wanted your day in court. Congratulations. The other side gets one too.** #KashPatel #FBI #DOJ #TheAtlantic #Discovery #LegalSatire #PoliticalHumor #FAFO #TrumpAdministration #Imgur

item.title: Thomas Massie’s resolution to impeach Pete Hegseth fails in the House 211-204, after 11 Democrats failed to show up for the vote.
item.description:
If those 11 Democrats had showed up, Hegseth would have been impeached 215-211.
The Republican-controlled House voted 211-204 on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, to block an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, sending eight articles accusing him of unlawful military operations and abuse of power to the House Judiciary Committee. Eleven Democrats were among 18 lawmakers who did not vote. Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, who introduced the impeachment resolution, was the only Republican to oppose referring the charges to committee. All 203 Democrats who voted joined him, while 210 Republicans and independent Rep. Kevin Kiley of California supported the motion. The 11 Democrats recorded as not voting were:
Julia Brownley, Lou Correa and Nancy Pelosi of California
Laura Gillen of New York
Steven Horsford of Nevada
Jonathan Jackson of Illinois
Brittany Pettersen of Colorado
Melanie Stansbury of New Mexico
Haley Stevens of Michigan
Marilyn Strickland of Washington
Frederica Wilson of Florida.
The vote prevented Massie from forcing separate House votes on the impeachment charges, effectively ending his effort during the current Congress. Hegseth remains defense secretary, with the resolution referred to the Judiciary Committee. Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment Monday, accusing Hegseth of violating federal law and constitutional limits on military authority during operations in Iran, Yemen and Venezuela. The resolution also alleged unlawful killings during strikes against suspected drug-trafficking vessels, failures to protect civilians and retaliation against Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona over his statements about unlawful military orders.
The impeachment process requires a simple majority in the House to approve at least one article, followed by a Senate trial where a two-thirds vote is necessary for conviction and removal from office. Tuesday's procedural vote prevented the charges from advancing to that stage. The eight articles remain before the House Judiciary Committee. Democrats could introduce a new impeachment resolution when the next Congress convenes in January, with Jeffries already on record supporting the effort against Hegseth.
"None of these are high crimes or misdemeanors," Hegseth argued. "They're partisan policy disagreements from people who want to politicize our military." President Trump mocked the impeachment effort, saying it "miserably FAILED!" Only two Cabinet secretaries in U.S. history have been impeached. Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached over a corruption scandal in 1876, and Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas was impeached over his handling of the southern border in 2024. Belknap was acquitted by the Senate, while Mayorkas had his charges dismissed.

The 1% stat in question, yes this was peer reviewed and published, in 2024. https://www.nature.com/articles/s44222-024-00253-7 Other supplemental reading for women's health disparities: https://www.weforum.org/stories/health-and-healthcare-systems/what-comes-next-for-women-health https://www.gavi.org/vaccineswork/5-conditions-highlight-womens-health-gap https://www.aamc.org/news/why-we-know-so-little-about-women-s-health Also, a micro post on the data in question. My apologies for attitude, I had a bias of thinking it wS more common knowledge. When I formation surprises us or seems unbelievable, it does the service of revealing our own biases and defaults. Also a history of racism in science: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_racism None of this is to attack science as an industry. This is to demonstrate *some* (not nearly all) of the political impacts on scientific work. Trying to remove politics from a conversation is a massive blind spot with deleterious effects. Cheers all thanks for the convos Editedit: check out Stand Up For Science for local chapters, national news, articles and ways to support scientists standing up against political abuse
